tagline: The prophet who watched Jerusalem fall, pleading with a people who would not listen and promising a new covenant written on the heart.
overview:
Jeremiah is the book of a prophet who lived through the end of the world as his people knew it. Called as a young man in the reign of King Josiah, he spoke for about forty years while the kingdom of Judah slid from reform into denial, from denial into rebellion, and from rebellion into ruin. He warned that the Babylonian army would come from the north, that the temple would not save a people who broke the covenant, and that the only way to live was to surrender. He was beaten, jailed, thrown into a muddy cistern, and called a traitor. Then everything he said came true: in 587 or 586 BC the Babylonians burned the temple and carried the people into exile.

The book is not arranged as a tidy biography. It gathers poems of judgment, prose sermons, stories about the prophet's arrests and trials, symbolic acts (a ruined linen belt, a smashed clay jar, a wooden yoke), letters to the exiles, oracles against the nations, and a handful of raw, private prayers in which Jeremiah argues with God. At its heart, in chapters 30 to 33, stands a small book of comfort that promises restoration after judgment and, in 31:31-34, a new covenant in which God will write his law on his people's hearts and forgive their sins.

Jeremiah matters because it refuses both cheap hope and final despair. It tells the truth about sin and its consequences without flinching, and it lets a faithful man weep, doubt, and complain in God's presence. The New Testament hears in its new covenant the promise Jesus fulfilled at the Last Supper.
author:
The book names its prophet as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth, a village in the territory of Benjamin a few miles north of Jerusalem (1:1). The book itself tells how his words came to be written down. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim (about 605 BC), Jeremiah dictated his oracles to Baruch son of Neriah, a scribe, who read the scroll in the temple; when the king cut it up and burned it, Jeremiah dictated a second scroll with many words added (chapter 36). Baruch appears as Jeremiah's companion, witness, and secretary (chapters 32, 36, 43, and 45), and many scholars think he, or scribes like him, gave the book much of its shape.

Modern study has long noticed three kinds of material: poetic oracles, prose stories told about Jeremiah in the third person, and prose sermons whose style closely resembles Deuteronomy and the books of Kings. Sigmund Mowinckel's classification of these as sources A, B, and C (1914) framed much later discussion. Some scholars attribute the prose sermons to later editors in the tradition of Deuteronomy writing during the exile; others argue they preserve Jeremiah's own preaching in the formal prose style of his day. Most agree that the book grew over time from the prophet's words, gathered by those close to him, and that it reached its final form after his death.
date:
Jeremiah's ministry began in the thirteenth year of Josiah (1:2), about 627 BC, and continued past the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC into the prophet's last days in Egypt (chapters 43 and 44). The first written collection dates to about 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim (chapter 36). The Hebrew book's final chapter reports the release of the exiled King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile, about 561 BC (52:31), so the book as we have it was completed no earlier than that. Scholars who see extensive later editing place its completion in the exile or soon after, and the existence of two different editions (see below) shows that the book was still being copied and arranged in more than one form for some time.

A few readers take the thirteenth year of Josiah as the date of Jeremiah's birth rather than his call, noting that the book records few oracles clearly datable to Josiah's reign, but most take 1:2 at its word as the start of his prophetic work.
setting:
Jeremiah lived through the collapse of one empire and the rise of another. When he was called, Assyria was failing. Josiah, king of Judah from about 640 to 609 BC, used the moment to purge idolatry and centralize worship in Jerusalem, a reform that gathered force after a book of the law was found in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kings 22-23). Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. In 609 Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt, and Egypt briefly controlled Judah, replacing Josiah's son Jehoahaz with his brother Jehoiakim. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish on the Euphrates (46:2), and Judah became Babylon's vassal.

Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC) rebelled, died as the Babylonians came, and his son Jehoiachin surrendered Jerusalem in 597 BC; the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the period, records the city's capture. Jehoiachin, the royal family, and many leading citizens (among them Ezekiel) were deported. Nebuchadnezzar set up Zedekiah (597 to 586 BC), whom Jeremiah urged to submit. Zedekiah rebelled, trusting Egypt, and the Babylonians besieged Jerusalem, broke through, and burned the city and temple. Clay letters found at Lachish in the 1930s, written by a Judean officer in those last months, give a glimpse of the collapse. Afterward the Babylonians appointed Gedaliah as governor; his assassination drove a remnant to flee to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them.
purpose:
The book was preserved for a people who had lost their land, king, and temple and needed to know why. It answers that the disaster was not the failure of Judah's God but his judgment on a people who broke his covenant, worshiped other gods, trusted in the temple as a charm, oppressed the poor, and refused every warning. That explanation vindicates God and calls the survivors to honest repentance rather than blaming their fathers or their fate.

The book also gives the exiles a future. It tells them to settle in Babylon and seek its welfare (chapter 29), promises a return after seventy years, and holds out a restored people, a righteous branch from David's line, and a new covenant. And by preserving Jeremiah's own anguished prayers, it teaches readers in any age how to stay faithful when obedience brings suffering.
story:
Jeremiah stands at the hinge of the Old Testament story, where the kingdom of Judah ends and the exile begins. Behind him lie the promises to Abraham, the covenant at Sinai with its blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28), and the long history of kings told in Samuel and Kings. His ministry overlaps with that of Zephaniah and Habakkuk, and in its later years with Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. Lamentations, placed after Jeremiah in the Christian Old Testament, mourns the fallen city.

What Jeremiah announces, Kings and Chronicles narrate, and the books of Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah pick up the story of exile and return; Ezra 1:1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22 explicitly present Cyrus's decree as the fulfillment of the word spoken through Jeremiah.
christ:
Jeremiah points to Christ in three main ways. First, his new covenant promise (31:31-34) is the Old Testament passage the New Testament most directly claims as fulfilled: Jesus speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews 8 quotes the promise in full as the covenant Christ mediates. Second, Jeremiah promises a righteous branch from David's line who will reign wisely and be called The LORD Our Righteousness (23:5-6; 33:15-16), a hope Christians see met in Jesus the son of David.

Third, Jeremiah's own life foreshadows Jesus's. He wept over Jerusalem, warned that the temple had become a den of robbers (7:11, words Jesus used as he cleared the temple in Matthew 21:13), was rejected by his own people, and suffered for speaking God's word. Some in Jesus's day even wondered whether he was Jeremiah (Matthew 16:14). This link is a pattern rather than a prediction: the suffering prophet prepares us to recognize the greater prophet who suffered for others.
reading:
Jeremiah is long and not strictly chronological, so it helps to read with a map of its parts and the kings' names in mind. Watch for the shifts between poetry (usually God's own voice or the prophet's lament) and prose (sermons and stories), and notice how often the speaker blurs, so that God, the prophet, and the ruined land seem to weep with one voice. The so-called confessions of Jeremiah (11:18-12:6; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18) are private complaints unlike anything else in the prophets; read them as permitted, honest prayer rather than as models of calm faith.

Two cautions help. Jeremiah's call to surrender to Babylon was a specific word for a specific moment, not a general rule about politics. And the famous promise of plans for welfare and hope (29:11) was spoken to a community facing seventy years of exile, most of whom would die before it came true; it is a promise to God's people through suffering, not a guarantee of individual success.

Readers should also know that Jeremiah survives in two editions. The Greek translation (the Septuagint, the Jewish translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in the last centuries BC) is about one-seventh shorter than the traditional Hebrew text, lacks some passages entirely (such as 33:14-26), and places the oracles against the nations after 25:13 in a different order. Fragments from the Dead Sea Scrolls include copies that match each form. Many scholars, following Emanuel Tov and others, think the Greek reflects an earlier Hebrew edition that was later expanded; others think the Greek translator or his source abbreviated. English Bibles follow the longer Hebrew text.

structure.title: The call of the prophet
structure.summary: God appoints Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations, gives him two visions (an almond branch and a boiling pot tilting from the north), and promises to stand with him against all opposition.

structure.title: Warnings and judgment on Judah
structure.summary: Poems and sermons expose Judah's unfaithfulness, attack false trust in the temple, and announce disaster from the north. Symbolic acts, the prophet's confessions, and words to the kings run through this section, which ends with the cup of God's wrath and the prediction of seventy years under Babylon.

structure.title: Conflict with priests and prophets
structure.summary: Jeremiah is put on trial for his temple sermon, wears a yoke to urge submission to Babylon, confronts the prophet Hananiah, and writes to the exiles telling them to settle in Babylon.

structure.title: The book of comfort
structure.summary: Promises of restoration: the return of the exiles, Rachel's weeping answered, the new covenant, Jeremiah's purchase of a field as a sign of the future, and the righteous branch of David.

structure.title: The last days of Jerusalem and after
structure.summary: Stories of the siege, the burned scroll, Jeremiah's imprisonment, the fall of the city, the murder of Gedaliah, and the flight to Egypt, closing with a word of assurance to Baruch.

structure.title: Oracles against the nations
structure.summary: Judgments on Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam, and at greatest length Babylon itself, the instrument of judgment that will in turn be judged.

structure.title: The fall of Jerusalem retold
structure.summary: A historical appendix, closely parallel to 2 Kings 24-25, recounts the city's destruction and ends with the release of King Jehoiachin in Babylon, a small light at the close of the book.

themes.title: Covenant broken and made new
themes.body: Jeremiah reads Judah's history through the covenant made at Sinai. The people have broken it by worshiping other gods and by injustice, and the curses Deuteronomy warned of are falling. Yet the book looks past the broken covenant to a new one, in which God himself will change hearts, forgive sin, and bind his people to himself permanently. Judgment is not God's last word; it clears ground for something he will build and plant.

themes.title: False security
themes.body: Again and again Jeremiah attacks the things Judah trusted instead of God: the temple as a guarantee, alliances with Egypt, the reassuring words of prophets who promised peace, and religious ritual without obedience. The book is a sustained warning that the forms of faith can become a hiding place from God himself.

themes.title: The true and false prophet
themes.body: Jeremiah is surrounded by prophets who say what kings and crowds want to hear. The book presses the question of how to tell a true word from a false one, and its answer involves the content of the message (does it call people to repentance?), the prophet's life, and finally whether the word comes to pass. Jeremiah's lonely faithfulness against popular religion is one of the book's central dramas.

themes.title: Suffering and honest prayer
themes.body: No other prophet lets us hear so much of his own pain. Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him, curses the day he was born, and begs for vindication, yet he keeps speaking the word he cannot hold in. The book shows that faithfulness can include lament and protest brought directly to God, and that God answers such prayer, sometimes with comfort and sometimes with a call to stand firm.

themes.title: God over the nations
themes.body: Jeremiah is appointed a prophet to the nations, and the book insists that the God of little Judah governs empires. Babylon is his servant for a season, the nations drink the cup of his wrath, and Babylon itself will fall. History is not the story of whichever army is strongest; it is the arena of God's purposes.

keyChapters.why: The call of Jeremiah, known before birth and sent to uproot and to plant, sets the terms for his whole ministry.
The temple sermon attacks trust in the temple as a charm and calls it a den of robbers, words Jesus later used.
The last and darkest of Jeremiah's confessions, where he feels deceived by God yet cannot stop speaking his word.
Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to build houses, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait for God's promised return.
The promise of a new covenant written on the heart, the Old Testament passage the New Testament most clearly claims as fulfilled in Christ.
King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, and the word of God is written again, a vivid picture of how the book itself came to be.
The fall of Jerusalem retold, closing with the release of the exiled king as a small sign that God's promise to David is not dead.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Jeremiah stands at the hinge of the Old Testament story, where the kingdom of Judah ends and the exile begins. Behind him lie the promises to Abraham, the covenant at Sinai with its promises and curses in Deuteronomy 28, and the long history of kings told in Samuel and Kings. Lamentations, which follows Jeremiah in the Christian Old Testament, mourns the fallen city.

What Jeremiah announces, Kings and Chronicles narrate. Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah pick up the story of exile and return, and both Ezra 1:1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22 present the decree of Cyrus as the fulfillment of the word spoken through Jeremiah. Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years in his own prayer in Daniel 9.

The book's last chapter retells the fall of Jerusalem in words close to 2 Kings 24 and 25, and it ends with a small light: the exiled King Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon and eats at the king's table. The line of David is humbled, but it has not ended.

The book names its prophet as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth, a village in the land of Benjamin a few miles north of Jerusalem (1:1). It also tells how his words came to be written. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, about 605 BC, Jeremiah dictated his oracles to Baruch son of Neriah, a scribe, who read the scroll in the temple. When the king cut it up and burned it, Jeremiah dictated a second scroll with many words added (chapter 36). Baruch appears as Jeremiah's companion, witness and secretary, and many scholars think he, or scribes like him, gave the book much of its shape.

Modern study has long noticed three kinds of material in the book: poetic oracles, prose stories told about Jeremiah, and prose sermons whose style is close to Deuteronomy and Kings. Sigmund Mowinckel's sorting of these into three sources in 1914 framed much later discussion. Some scholars give the prose sermons to later editors during the exile. Others argue they keep Jeremiah's own preaching in the formal prose of his day. Most agree that the book grew from the prophet's words, gathered by those close to him, and reached its final form after his death.

Jeremiah's ministry began in the thirteenth year of Josiah (1:2), about 627 BC, and continued past the fall of Jerusalem into his last days in Egypt. The last chapter reports the release of Jehoiachin in about 561 BC, so the book was completed no earlier than that.

Jeremiah survives in two forms. The Greek translation, the Septuagint, made by Jews in the last centuries BC, is about one seventh shorter than the traditional Hebrew text. It lacks some passages entirely, such as 33:14-26, and it places the oracles against the nations after 25:13, in a different order. Fragments among the Dead Sea Scrolls include copies that match each form.

Many scholars, following Emanuel Tov and others, think the Greek reflects an earlier Hebrew edition that was later expanded. Others think the Greek translator or his source shortened the book. English Bibles follow the longer Hebrew text, and so do these notes.

The two editions show that the book was still being copied and arranged in more than one form for some time. They do not change its message. Both tell the same story of warning, ruin and promise. They are a reminder that the prophet's words were treasured and handed on by a community that kept working with them, much as the burned scroll of chapter 36 was written again with words added.

parts.h: Josiah, the kings after him, and Babylon
parts.body:
Jeremiah lived through the collapse of one empire and the rise of another. When he was called, Assyria was failing. Josiah, king of Judah from about 640 to 609 BC, used the moment to clear away idolatry and gather worship to Jerusalem, a reform that gathered force after a book of the law was found in the temple in 622 BC. Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. In 609 Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho II, and Egypt briefly controlled Judah, replacing Josiah's son Jehoahaz with his brother Jehoiakim.

In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish on the Euphrates (46:2), and Judah became Babylon's subject. Jehoiakim, who reigned from 609 to 598 BC, rebelled and died as the Babylonians came. His son Jehoiachin surrendered Jerusalem in 597 BC, and the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the period, records the city's capture. Jehoiachin, the royal family and many leading citizens, Ezekiel among them, were taken away.

Nebuchadnezzar set up Zedekiah, who reigned from 597 to 586 BC, and Jeremiah urged him to submit. Zedekiah rebelled, trusting Egypt, and the Babylonians besieged Jerusalem, broke through and burned the city and temple. Clay letters found at Lachish in the 1930s, written by a Judean officer in those last months, give a glimpse of the collapse. Afterward Babylon appointed Gedaliah governor. His murder drove a remnant to flee to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them.

The book moves in large blocks rather than in strict order of time. Chapter 1 is the call: God appoints Jeremiah over nations and kingdoms ‘to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant’ (1:10). Those six verbs are the book in small. Four of them tear down, and two build.

Chapters 2 to 25 are warnings and judgment on Judah: poems and sermons that expose the people's unfaithfulness, attack false trust in the temple and announce disaster from the north. The prophet's private prayers, the acted signs and words to the kings run through them, and the section ends with the cup of God's wrath and seventy years under Babylon.

Chapters 26 to 29 tell of conflict with priests and prophets: Jeremiah on trial for his temple sermon, the yoke he wore, his clash with the prophet Hananiah, and his letter telling the exiles to settle in Babylon. Chapters 30 to 33 are the book of comfort. Chapters 34 to 45 tell the last days of Jerusalem and after, closing with a word to Baruch. Chapters 46 to 51 are oracles against the nations, ending with Babylon. Chapter 52 retells the fall of the city.

Watch for the shifts between poetry, usually God's voice or the prophet's lament, and prose, the sermons and stories. Notice how often the speaker blurs, so that God, the prophet and the ruined land seem to weep with one voice.

parts.h: A covenant broken, and false security
parts.body:
Jeremiah reads Judah's history through the covenant made at Sinai. The people have broken it by worshiping other gods and by injustice, and the curses Deuteronomy warned of are falling. God's charge in chapter 2 sets the tone: ‘They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns’ (2:13).

Again and again Jeremiah attacks what Judah trusted instead of God. The temple was the first of these. In the temple sermon of chapter 7 he warns, ‘Do not trust in deceptive words’ (7:4), and asks whether God's house has become a den of robbers (7:11). Alliances with Egypt were another. So were the soothing words of prophets who promised peace when there was no peace, and religious ritual without obedience.

The book is a long warning that the forms of faith can become a hiding place from God himself. That warning is not aimed at a people outside the faith. It was spoken by a priest's son to his own people in the temple courts, and every generation of believers stands under it. These notes read Jeremiah's judgments on Judah as Judah's own Scripture, never as a reason to blame the Jewish people, and never as a key for calling any people's suffering deserved.

No other prophet lets readers hear so much of his own pain. Scattered through chapters 11 to 20 are five private prayers, often called the confessions of Jeremiah (11:18-12:6; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18). In them Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper, complains that he has become a man of strife, calls God a deceptive brook, prays harsh prayers against those who plot to kill him, and finally curses the day he was born.

They are not models of calm faith, and the book does not present them that way. They are permitted, honest prayer. In them a faithful man brings his anger and despair straight to God, and God answers, sometimes with comfort and sometimes with a call to stand firm and speak again. In chapter 20 Jeremiah says that when he tries to keep silent, God's word becomes ‘a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones’ (20:9).

The last confession ends in darkness, and the plain notes on chapter 20 handle it with the same care as the notes on Job 3.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Jeremiah is surrounded by prophets who say what kings and crowds want to hear. They promise peace, a quick return from exile and the broken power of Babylon. Chapter 23 attacks them for speaking visions from their own minds, and chapter 28 tells of Hananiah, who broke the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck and promised that the exiles would be home within two years.

The book presses the question of how to tell a true word from a false one, and its answer has several parts. A true prophet calls people to turn from evil, while false prophets strengthen the hands of evildoers. A true prophet stands in the LORD's council and does not simply repeat what the listeners want. And in the end, a word is shown to be true when it comes to pass. Both kinds of prophet said ‘declares the LORD’, so the hearers had to weigh the message itself.

Jeremiah's lonely faithfulness against popular religion is one of the book's central dramas. It is not a story of a good outsider against bad insiders. Jeremiah was a priest's son and spoke in the temple courts. The struggle was within the people of God.

parts.h: Seek the peace of the city
parts.body:
In 597 BC many of Judah's leaders were already in Babylon. Prophets there promised a quick return. Jeremiah wrote them a letter (chapter 29) telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry and have children, and ‘Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles’ (29:7). They were to pray for Babylon, because their own welfare was bound up with it. God would bring them home, but only after seventy years.

The same letter holds the most quoted verse in the book: ‘For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope’ (29:11). It was spoken to a whole community facing seventy years of exile, most of whom would die before it came true. It is a promise to God's people through suffering, not a guarantee of an individual's success, and it does not promise anyone that hardship will not come.

Jeremiah's call to surrender to Babylon was a word for a particular moment, given to particular kings. It is not a general rule about politics, and it is not a rule that God always wants submission to an oppressor. The book itself turns to judge Babylon in chapters 50 and 51.

parts.h: Rachel's tears and the new covenant
parts.body:
Chapters 30 to 33 are a small book of comfort set in the middle of the book of ruin. Jeremiah hears Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeping in Ramah for her children who are gone, and God tells her to stop weeping, because they will come back (31:15-17). While the Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem, Jeremiah buys a field in Anathoth and seals the deed in a clay jar, a sign that houses and fields will again be bought in the land (chapter 32).

Then comes the promise the New Testament claims more directly than almost any other. God will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the one they broke. ‘I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people’ (31:33). Everyone will know the LORD, and he will forgive their sins.

Jesus took the cup at the Last Supper and called it ‘the new covenant in My blood’ (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews 8 quotes the promise in full. Christians differ on how the promise to Israel and Judah reaches the church, and Jewish readers have read it as the covenant of Sinai at last kept faithfully. The plain notes on chapter 31 set out those readings. None of them gives anyone room for contempt toward the Jewish people, to whom the promise was first made.

Jeremiah was appointed a prophet to the nations (1:5), and chapters 46 to 51 speak to them: Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam, and at greatest length Babylon itself. The God of little Judah governs empires. Babylon is his servant for a season, the nations drink the cup of his wrath, and then Babylon falls.

These oracles are hard reading. Some call for whole armies to be destroyed, and some picture God's judgment as a sacrifice or a harvest. They are poetry of judgment on ancient powers for their pride and cruelty. Yet the same chapters show God weeping for Moab (48:31-36) and promising to restore Moab, Ammon and Elam in later days.

The oracles against Babylon close with a scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates, a sign that Babylon would sink and never rise (51:63-64). Babylon was taken by Cyrus in 539 BC almost without a battle, and the plain notes on chapters 50 and 51 say how readers have weighed that against the poems.

These words concern Egypt, Moab, Edom and Babylon as ancient nations. These notes draw no line from them to any nation or state of the present day.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Jeremiah
parts.body:
The New Testament draws on Jeremiah in a few clear places. The new covenant of 31:31-34 is the plainest. Jesus speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews 8 quotes the promise in full as the covenant Christ mediates, and returns to it in Hebrews 10.

When Jesus cleared the temple, he joined Isaiah's house of prayer with Jeremiah's den of robbers (7:11; Matthew 21:13). Matthew reads Rachel weeping in Ramah beside the grief of Bethlehem's mothers when Herod killed their children (31:15; Matthew 2:17-18). Paul takes up the one thing worth boasting in, to know the LORD (9:24), when he writes, ‘Let him who boasts boast in the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Some in Jesus' day wondered whether he was Jeremiah (Matthew 16:14). Readers have long noticed the likeness: a prophet who wept over Jerusalem, warned that the temple had become a den of robbers, and was rejected by his own people. The New Testament does not call that likeness a prediction, and these notes draw no line from Jeremiah to Christ that the New Testament does not draw itself.

Jeremiah is long and not strictly in order of time, so read with a map of its parts and the kings' names in mind: Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. When a chapter gives a date, use it to place the chapter in the story.

Read the poems slowly, and let the pictures work: the broken cisterns, the almond branch, the potter's wheel, the balm in Gilead. Read the prose stories as stories, with their tension and their cost. Read the confessions as prayer, not as doctrine.

Some passages are very hard. Jeremiah's poems picture faithless Judah as an unfaithful wife and a woman exposed. These are pictures of a city and a covenant, and they give no warrant for any man to shame or harm any woman. Some passages name the horrors of the siege, and these notes name them without describing them. The oracles against the nations call for judgment on ancient powers, and they draw no line to any people today.

Above all, read Jeremiah as the book of a man who would not stop telling the truth, and of a God who, after uprooting and tearing down, promised to build and to plant.

No descendant of Coniah on David's throne, and Matthew's genealogy.
How the seventy years add up, and how to read the number.
Submit to Babylon: a word for one moment, not a rule that God wants submission to every oppressor.
Plans to prosper you: a promise to a people in exile, not a guarantee of personal success.
A new covenant with Israel and Judah: Jewish and Christian readings, with no room for contempt.
Child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom, something God says never entered his mind.
The Queen of Heaven: when experience seems to argue against God.
A curse on whoever holds back the sword, while God weeps for Moab.
Babylon never inhabited again, though Cyrus took it almost without a battle.
Calls for Babylon's destruction: judgment on an ancient empire, no line to any nation today.

words.line: The binding bond between God and his people, broken at Sinai's terms and promised new in 31:31-34.
Jeremiah's key word, used for turning back to God and for coming home from exile (3:12; 30:3).
Well-being; the false prophets cried peace when there was none (6:14), and the exiles were to seek the city's peace (29:7).
The six verbs of Jeremiah's call, four to tear down and two to build (1:10), echoed through the book (31:28).
The seat of will and thought: deceitful above all things (17:9), and the place where the new covenant is written (31:33).
Jeremiah's phrase for walking by one's own plans instead of God's word (7:24; 9:14).
Falsehood, Jeremiah's word for false prophets and false trust (7:4; 28:15).
A pit cut to hold rainwater; Judah dug broken ones (2:13), and Jeremiah was dropped into one (38:6).
The righteous shoot God will raise up for David, whose name says the LORD is his people's righteousness (23:5-6; 33:15).
The direction of the coming disaster, a boiling pot tilting from the north (1:13-14).
Those left after judgment, whom God will gather again (23:3).
The wooden bar Jeremiah wore as a sign of submission to Babylon, broken by Hananiah (27:2; 28:10).
A healing resin from Gilead; the prophet asks why his people are not healed (8:22).
The time of Babylon's rule (25:11; 29:10), read again by Daniel (Daniel 9:2).
The picture of judgment handed to the nations to drink (25:15).

timeline.what: Josiah becomes king of Judah as a boy.
In Josiah's thirteenth year, the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah (1:2).
A book of the law is found in the temple, and Josiah's reform gathers force (2 Kings 22 and 23).
Nineveh, Assyria's capital, falls to the Babylonians and Medes.
Josiah is killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho II; Egypt puts Jehoiakim on the throne.
Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish (46:2). Jeremiah dictates his scroll to Baruch, and Jehoiakim burns it (chapter 36).
Jehoiachin surrenders Jerusalem; the king, the royal family and many leaders, Ezekiel among them, are taken to Babylon.
Jeremiah writes to the exiles to settle in Babylon and seek its peace (chapter 29), and confronts Hananiah (chapter 28).
Babylon besieges Jerusalem. Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth (chapter 32) and is thrown into a cistern (chapter 38).
Jerusalem falls; the city and temple are burned (chapters 39 and 52).
Letters on clay found at Lachish, written by a Judean officer in the last months, are published.
Gedaliah governs at Mizpah and is murdered; a remnant flees to Egypt, taking Jeremiah (chapters 40 to 43).
The exiled King Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon (52:31); the book is completed no earlier than this.
Cyrus allows the exiles to return; Ezra 1:1 calls it the fulfillment of the word spoken through Jeremiah.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The city of the temple sermon (7:2), besieged and burned (39:8).

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: The survivors stopped near Bethlehem on their way to Egypt (41:17).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: Zedekiah was overtaken in the plains of Jericho as he fled (39:5).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: The northern shrine whose trust shamed Israel (48:13).

places.name: Shechem
places.line: Mourners came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria to bring offerings after the fall (41:5).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan known for its balm: ‘Is there no balm in Gilead?’ (8:22). Drawn roughly, as a region.

places.name: Philistia
places.line: The Philistine coast of chapter 47. Drawn roughly, as a region with its name only.

places.name: Moab
places.line: The land east of the Dead Sea, judged and wept over in chapter 48. Drawn roughly, as a region with its name only.

places.name: Edom
places.line: The land south and east of the Dead Sea (49:7-22). Drawn roughly, as a region with its name only; no people of the present day is meant.

places.name: Tyre
places.line: The Phoenician port named with Sidon in the word against the Philistines (47:4).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Capital of Aram, the subject of 49:23-27.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Judah's capital, between the two powers.

places.name: Egypt
places.line: The power Judah kept turning to (2:18), where the last survivors fled with Jeremiah (43:7). Drawn roughly, as a region with its name only.

places.name: Babylon
places.line: The city whose peace the exiles were to seek (29:7), and which would sink and never rise (51:64). Drawn at its ruin mounds near Hillah.

teaching.mapNote: Ancient sites are placed at their ruin mounds; Gilead, Philistia, Moab, Edom and Egypt are drawn roughly, as regions with names only. Anathoth, Mizpah, Ramah, Lachish, Tahpanhes, Carchemish and Elam are left off, because the site's records do not place them. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
